title: Job
note:
Built from the curriculum photographs in Drive’s Beginner → Chapter 15 → “01 - Curriculum Source”: three pages, p.67 (title, prayer, Bible portion), p.68 (the lesson) and p.69 (“Tell the Answers”, “Find the Correct Answer” and a picture activity).

**p.70 is still not in Drive, and it is the page with the Memory Verse on it.** The curriculum folder holds exactly three photographs, p.67 to p.69; the chapter’s “06 - Memory Verse” folder is empty; and the thirteen artwork panels carry no memory-verse card, where Chapter 14’s last panel printed its verse in full. So this chapter still has no `verse`, no `decision` and no `song`, all of which are printed on p.70. The verse is never guessed. One photograph of p.70 is all it needs.

`prayer` carries the **opening** prayer from p.67, which is printed in full here. Chapters 12 and 14 went the other way — their opening prayer was a stage direction and `prayer` carried the Concluding Prayer instead. This is the first chapter where it is reversed, and only because the closing page is missing.

**Artwork.** Thirteen panels and both covers came from Drive’s “04 - Story Artwork”, all fifteen distinct by SHA-256. The folder was enumerated by exact filename rather than by paging, because the listing caps at five and its cursor repeats rows; querying each name confirmed panels 1 to 13 and the two covers, and no panel 14 or above. The twenty-two text cards this chapter first shipped with are gone rather than reconciled, which is what happened to Beginner Chapters 5 to 14 and to Primary 1 to 3: the panels letter their own captions and speech, so a card that repeated them underneath would print the same sentence twice. Each card is now a picture with `alt` describing the scene and quoting what is lettered on it.

Panel 1 is 940×1672, one pixel narrow of the canonical 941×1672. Converted without distortion and nothing resized it; recorded rather than fixed, since a one-pixel difference is invisible and the artwork is the teacher’s.

**The artwork answers both of the questions flagged against p.69 when the games shipped.** “Find the Correct Answer” 4 offers “Offer sacrifices/feast” where the lesson said Job would “gather his children together, and pray to forgive them”; panel 11 letters “After the feast, Job gathered his children and offered sacrifices to God for them”, and panel 8 letters “After the meal, Job prayed for each of his children” — so the artwork has him do both, and the printed answer is “Offer sacrifices”. “Find the Correct Answer” 3 asks whether the brothers invited their sisters; the lesson still never says, but panels 5 to 7 draw the daughters at the table with everyone else, which supports “invited”. The games were left on the lesson’s own words and did not need changing. Both remain the teacher’s call to confirm, now with the artwork as evidence.

cover.note: Both drawn and imported, both at the canonical sizes — 941×1672 portrait and 1672×941 landscape.

story.alt: A boy lies on a cushion on the living-room rug with his chin in his hands, grinning up at Halo. Behind him his father reads from a Bible on the sofa while his mother and little sister listen. The boy says, “My family loves being together!” and Halo asks, “Do you pray together, too?”
The same room, a big open Bible on the floor in front of the boy now. He says, “Hmm… We don’t always remember to pray together.” Halo answers, “That’s something we can learn about!”

A glowing vision unfurls out of the open Bible: a bearded man in a blue robe standing with a staff among his family, with sheep and cattle on the green hills behind. Halo says, “I know a story about a man named Job!” and the boy asks, “Wow! What was he like?”

Job stands outside his stone house with all ten of his children crowded around him, every one of them looking up at him, the flocks grazing on the hillside behind. The caption reads, “Job had seven sons and three daughters. He had a very large family!”

A long table laid with dishes under lanterns at dusk, Job in the middle of his grown sons and daughters. The caption reads, “Job’s children often came together at each other’s homes for special meals and to be with their father.”

Job stands at the head of the table holding up a cup, his children raising theirs back, the table loaded with food and the courtyard lit by lanterns. The caption reads, “Job made a big meal for them. They would eat, celebrate, and be happy together as a family.”

The meal is over and the family is making music — one son plays a stringed instrument, a daughter holds a tambourine, the rest clap. The caption reads, “They enjoyed the meal and spent time together. Job was so happy to see his children united and loving one another.”

Job kneels with his hands pressed together and his eyes closed, and all around him his children kneel and bow their heads the same way, lanterns burning low beside them. The caption reads, “After the meal, Job prayed for each of his children.”

Job stands in a wide green pasture with his shepherd’s crook, one hand resting on the head of an ox, sheep crowding round his feet and camels and a donkey behind him. The caption reads, “Job also took care of many animals. He had sheep, camels, cattle, and donkeys.”

Job sits on a low stone wall at sunset with his hand at his chin, watching his grown children talking together across the courtyard. The caption reads, “Job loved his children. He wanted them to do what was right and stay close to God.”

Job stands with both arms raised beside a stone altar with a fire burning on it, his children behind him with their hands folded and their eyes closed. The caption reads, “After the feast, Job gathered his children and offered sacrifices to God for them.”

Back in the living room, the boy sits cross-legged on the rug looking up at Halo, his family on the sofa behind. The caption reads, “Job loved his children and prayed for them. We can pray for our families, too!” Halo asks, “Who can you pray for in your family?” and the boy answers, “I can pray for Mummy, Daddy, and everyone at home!”

The whole family kneels together at the coffee table with their hands folded and their eyes closed, an open Bible in front of them and Halo glowing quietly at the end of the table. The caption reads, “Let us praise God, read the Bible, and pray together as a family!”

curriculum.source: Beginners Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 15 “Job”, p.69 — “Tell the Answers”
curriculum.note: All five questions transcribed from the printed page, punctuation and spacing included — the spaced question marks and the stray full stop in “What did Job do for his children.?” are the book’s, not a typo here. Every answer is in the lesson on p.68. The four “Find the Correct Answer” fill-ins on the same page are not recorded as questions: two of them are the same as questions 1 and 2 above, and the other two ask things the lesson does not answer, which the chapter note sets out.

questions.question: Where did Job live ?
questions.objective: Remember that Job lived in the land of Uz.
questions.answer: In the land of Uz. “They lived in the land of Uz.” (p.68)

questions.question: How many sons did Job have ?
questions.objective: Remember that Job had seven sons.
questions.answer: Seven. “He had a very large family consisting of three daughters, seven sons, his wife and many servants.” (p.68)

questions.question: Why did they gather together in one of their houses?
questions.objective: Remember that Job’s children gathered to feast together on special occasions.
questions.answer: To feast together on special occasions. “That day there would be feasting in that house. They would spend their time eating, drinking, cracking jokes with each other and sharing joy.” (p.68)

questions.question: Why would Job gather his children around ?
questions.objective: Remember that Job was worried his children might have sinned.
questions.answer: Because he was worried that one of them might have done wrong. “Job, who is God fearing, is worried whether any of his children would do any wrong.” (p.68)

questions.question: What did Job do for his children.?
questions.objective: Remember that Job prayed and asked God to forgive his children.
questions.answer: He prayed for them. “He would gather his children together, and pray to forgive them of any sins that they might have done knowingly or unknowingly.” (p.68)

games.title: Job's Big Family
games.objective: Remember that Job lived in the land of Uz and had seven sons.
games.note:
Two of the five printed questions in one board, because they are the two the lesson answers in its own opening sentences. The two extra pairs are not padding: “Three → How many daughters” sits beside “Seven → How many sons” so the number is remembered rather than guessed from being the only number on the board, and “Job → A man who loved God” is the lesson’s first description of him.

Shelf picture panel-03. The doorway into the Bible story — the vision unfurling out of the boy’s open Bible, with Halo saying “I know a story about a man named Job!”. Both bubbles survive the square crop whole. It names Job, which this board is not marked on, and shows neither a number nor the land. Panel 4 is the obvious picture for this game and is the one card it cannot have: its caption reads “Job had seven sons and three daughters”, which is two of the four pairs.

games.title: All in One House
games.objective: Remember that Job's children gathered in one house to feast together.

interactions.prompt: Why did they gather in one house?
interactions.hint: They ate, drank and shared joy.

games.note:
Both wrong options are made of things the lesson actually names — the cattle and livestock Job owned, and the many servants in his house — rather than other plausible reasons to gather. A child who remembers the feast picks it; a child who is guessing is guessing between three things that are all really in the story.

Renamed from “Feasting Together” when the artwork went in. The shelf prints a game’s title above its card and a child reads it before playing, so a game whose answer is “To feast together” cannot be called Feasting Together — the title was the answer. The new one restates the question instead.

Shelf picture panel-04. Job with all ten of his children outside his house. The caption is cropped away, so the card carries no lettering. The feast panels — 5, 6 and 7 — were all passed over even though their captions crop away too: a laden table above “Why did they gather in one house?” hands the answer over in the picture. Panel 9 was passed over for the opposite reason, that a card full of cattle sits right beside the wrong option “To count the cattle”.

games.title: After the Feast
games.objective: Remember what Job did for his children once the feasting was over.
games.note:
The sequence stops at “He prayed for them” and never says what he prayed for. The fourth game asks why he gathered them, and a step reading “he asked God to forgive their sins” would answer it before it is asked.

Shelf picture panel-10. Job alone on a low wall at sunset, watching his children. No lettering survives the crop and no step of the sequence is shown. Panels 5 to 8, 11 and 12 are all steps of this game — the feast, the praying, the gathering — and none of them could be used.

games.title: Why Job Prayed
games.objective: Remember that Job gathered his children because he worried they had sinned, and what the lesson asks every home to do.

interactions.prompt: Why did Job gather his children?
Turn over what we should do.

games.note:
The reason first, then what the lesson asks of the child. Both wrong options are the two things the chapter’s other games are about — cattle and feasting — so a child who is pattern-matching on “what was in this chapter” gets no help from it. The reveal is the lesson’s own closing paragraph, the four things it asks every home to do, and it answers nothing the game above it is marked on.

Shelf picture panel-13. The boy’s own family kneeling together at the coffee table, which is where this game lands. No lettering survives the crop. It shows the four things the reveal holds, but a reveal card cannot be wrong, so there is nothing here to give away — and the multiple choice above it, about what Job was worried about, gets no help from it at all.

video.title: Job
video.note: Supplied for the Watch screen as an embed; only the eleven-character id is kept. The `si=` parameter on the pasted URL is a YouTube share token that identifies where the link came from, and it has no business travelling into a children's app — the schema accepts the id alone, which is why it cannot. Served through youtube-nocookie.com, and nothing is embedded until a child asks to watch.

prayer.text: O our Creator God, we praise you for loving us. We thank you for our loved ones, our dear ones. Help us to pray and be happy with them. Amen
prayer.note: The opening prayer from p.67, word for word, printed in full rather than as a stage direction. It is the opening prayer and not the Concluding Prayer because p.70, which carries the closing of the lesson, is not in Drive.

celebration.message: Job prayed for his children, and the Lord blessed him.
celebration.note: The turn of the chapter, from p.68. The lesson is not about Job’s suffering — it names it in one sentence and moves on — but about the habit he kept: after every feast, he gathered his children and prayed.
